review:
Wolfenstein II is packed full of great and memorable moments, not only in the story it tells but also the combat it presents. From walking the streets of Roswell, New Mexico and seeing KKK members walking together with Nazis to sneaking up on an unexpected soldier only to gruesomely amputate and decapitate them before they could recite their favourite verse from Mein Kampf. 

It’s provocative and intense in equal measure. 

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

I have complicated feelings about the New Colossus. I have never wished for a middle option in Steam Reviews more. 

On the one hand, it's definitly more Wolfenstein. The series is a bit of a miracle that it exists and is offered to us in a complete package in this day and age.

But on the other hand, there's a really aweful sense of "And another thing" that hangs over the entire game. The New Order was about as close to perfect as a first person shooter can get, it was tightly packed, unexpected, came from no where, and ended in a satisfying manner. The New Colossus feels like it was brought back to life against its will, not unlike it's dour but loveable player character. 

There's just no *energy* here. There are only two new enemies, the nearly 3/5ths of the game takes place  in a horrible, endless sewer level, and the story feels both extremely padded and cut to pieces at the same time. And then it just ends right when it SHOULD be getting ready for Act III. It shamelessly retreads set-peices from the first game, and the stuff they do add runs from 'okay but under-developed' to 'jesus christ we GET IT CHILD ABUSE IS BAD'. The London Monitor fight may not have been perfect, but it was at least a set piece. The New Colossus keeps a steady, snails pace and then falls asleep barely out of the gate.

Time is not being kind to this game in my memory. I feel like eight of my fourteen hour play time was spent chewing through padding or wasting time in a sewer. For all the talk of igniting a revolution, you spend ninty percent of the game trying to rescue about twenty people and then...you win! Revolution Accomplished? The obvious sequel baiting is sickening, and for all the early buzz and ghoulish imagery of the KKK and Third Reich running the streets of America, very little is DONE with that Imagery or weighty ideas. It borders on a game about nothing, or more appropriately about being brought back when your job was done.

I realise as I write that I should be giving the game a thumbs down. There were moments of fun, but none strong enough to actually recommend it, not at $60.00. I didn't feel like my time was MALICIOUSLY wasted (al la Deus Ex: Mankind Divided), but I feel like a bunch of talented, intelligent, well meaning people looked at the well and realised they didn't have anything left to say about BJ Blazkowivc. That's what The New Colossus is to me: The bottom barrel scrape of the idea bucket.

I feel honestly terrible about this. I wanted to like The New Colossus. I loved The New Order dearly, and there WAS love and effort put into this game. But not enough, and not in the right places.

I think that myself and a lot of the people writing negative reviews may have played two different games.

I hear three main things: Bugs, weak story, political agenda.

Let me address the bugs first: The only one I experienced was a graphical bug that happened when explosions were onscreen. Black boxes would fill the screen and blind me. This was fixed by changing my AA and I never saw it again. Other than that, a pretty bug free experience.

As for the weak story, its pretty basic, but there are some twists and turns that I very much enjoyed. Engel is very much a hateable villain, and her pure evil never strays into being so comical you can't take her seriously. She's an unhinged psychopath and every time you deal with her your skin will crawl and you will seethe with hatred. There is one moment in the game where the story jerks you back to reality in a very unsubtle way and you become legitimately worried about what will happen next. I thought the story was pretty good for what it needed to do.

Finally... The claims of political agenda. I personally hate how political agendas have worked their way into damn near everything, and the massive controversy swirling around this game over that put me off playing this game for nearly a year until I finally decided that I was going to try it myself to see if it was true, and wouldn't you know it, the people whining about this game being politically biased are just as sensitive as the people they complain about. Everything in this game is genuine and accurate to its timeline. Anyone remember J from New Order? There is nothing in this game any more politically charged than the things he said. In fact, there is a rather stark moment in one of BJ's childhood flashbacks that lays the issue out plain: Two kids, both being taught hate by their parents for each other, become friends, unhindered by race, too innocent to understand the vitriol their respective sides pour out for the other. This is handled expertly. As for the game beating you over the head with "Nazis bad", I never felt that way. For me, it was just the bad guys doing bad guy things. If at any point you start feeling the need to defend Nazis, go have a conversation with yourself.

TL;DR: Game good. Story fine. Political controversy is drummed up nonexistent nonsense. Play game, enjoy.

Having thoroughly enjoyed both The New Order (TNO) and The Old Blood (TOB) I couldn't wait for this game to be released and continue the story of BJ.

However, if one was to ask me whether or not I would recommend this game to all Wolfenstein fans out there, or to anyone in general who likes a good shooter, as much as it saddens me the end result would have to be a 'no'.

The reasons for this negative outcome are threefold:
1. Whilst the story continues nicely from The New Order and Frau Engel is very effectively promoted from sidekick in TNO to the main antagonist in TNC the game has pacing issues. You're constantly fulfilling missions to rally people for the cause and incite a new rebellion and then.........the game suddenly ends. 

All the building up of tension, interaction between characters etc comes to a sudden and screeching halt and ends on a sudden low note. The third act of the game feels very rushed and doesn't give us a satisfying ending like was the case with the final battle in TNO. You don't feel like you're fighting alongside others, the very people you spent an inordinate amount of time on getting together. 

2. The game is bristling with characters but most of them are just filler, background noise. Bombate, Seth, Anya, Wyatt and Fergus are still the most interesting and memorable people you'll run into and the newly introduced characters in TNC pale by comparison. There are some that have a tragic and interesting background, like Sigrun Engel (daughter of Frau Engel) but their stories are mostly just briefly hinted/referenced at, rather than becoming an integral part of the story. It doesn't help that, unlike the central hub of TNO, the submarine you call your main base of operations in TNC feels far more devoid of life and seems needlessly complex/large to traverse. It looks awesome and the amount of attention to little details is amazing but it never feels like home when you come back from a mission.

3. The gunplay is far less interesting than it was in TNO. In that game, and in TOB, all guns had their place meaning all of them would have their frequent moments of use. In TNC I rarely used anything other than the pistol, assaultrifle and diesel/lasergun. The SMGs for example are completely useless as they are too inaccurate and just don't have enough stoppingpower. Speaking of actual gameplay: 3 DLC packages have also been released by MachineGames, which focus on other characters in the TNC universe, but all of these have been given poor ratings due to feeling like rehashed segments of the original game TNC.

Is TNC a bad game? Certainly not. Graphics, musics, sound effects, voice acting etc are all topnotch. Yet something is missing in this game, a certain amount of cohesion between the story that unfolds, the characters you meet and the actions you unleash upon the world you walk around in. It somehow feels rushed and underwhelming and doesn't leave the lasting impact that I felt when I had finished TNO.
Stomping Hitler in the skull and teabagging him for a couple of hours before moving forward with the main mission felt very wonderful. Kinda wish I did a little more tbh.

I played this uber-gorgeous, ultra-violent shooter in 2020 until it bricked my saves after 4 hours in. So, I refunded it, maddened, and Steam allowed it somehow. Recently, I repurchased the game, hoping for the best. Seen a couple of crashes, but this time I could go past Manhattan. God, I loved its post-nuclear vistas! I love all the vibrant gore, machine porn, and spectacular set pieces! The courtroom power fantasy alone... Soon, I realised the map's existence. By ignoring it I missed out on lots of fun stuff! Max Hass. So, I restarted again, then forgot about the map anyway, losing myself in the action. My odd persistence is a testament to how potent it is. The game f#cked me over, then I f#cked myself over with it, yet I kept playing. Here, I won't go into excruciating detail. After all, this entry closely resembles its predecessors, which everyone and my grandma played by now. I like New Order and Old Blood better, but this one is solid and there's a crucial distinction that makes it stand out. Before we get to it, I'd like to address the dogmatic cringe surrounding The New Colossus since the day it was built. Being socially critical by the nature of its story, it doesn't belong in the same trash heap of graceless hipster c#ntfiction as Veilguard or Dustborn.

[h3]Slop Machine[/h3]
But a false assumption makes everything possible. Let's assume that people who praise or call this game out for its political agenda are correct. Let's assume the prevalent role of women is a mocking statement and that the whole Nazi shtick is an allegorical spit in the face of all conservatives. Let's assume the badass wheelchair sequence is DEI virtue signalling and a fat Aryan Frau riding a BBC is BLM propaganda. Let's assume that some jokes don't land because they were trying too hard to insult you and yours, being too brainwashed by "The Matrix" to think of anything better than blatant accusations. Hell, let's assume this is the wokest game ever made, that it's unrestricted cultural warfare incarnate! I still couldn't care less because it's a first-class shooter that made my heart pump battery acid. Now, you can obediently swallow every rage bait from the corporate identity labs, blown out of proportion to mislead and debase both sides. Or you can stop being a constantly offended snitch, push away the slobbery udder shared with your ideological rival - and start chopping off limbs. It's not that deep.

But it's smart and direct, only misrepresented to serve the preachy slop machine. Don't look at me like that. Wolfenstein's story is pulpy and mostly played for laughs. It awkwardly downplays serious moments and jumps the sharks already jumped before. But it also emphasises redemption for those who can be redeemed and forgiveness from those who are strong enough to forgive. It ain't high art, yet I hate to see it twisted, warped beyond recognition. And I hate when we give up good things in life: good games, good words, or good people. Just because they don't align perfectly with every single dogma we might've internalised. We lose too much in the crossfire, demonising humans and phenomenons to absurdity for the slightest disparity. Some think this is what it means to be uncompromising, principled, aware. I thought so, too, looking for solace in endless anathemas. But there's no rest for the wicked. We don't have to be friends or some motherf#cking hippies, we won't ever agree on certain things. Alas, a complete inability to reconcile only shows a strategically imposed cultic mindset of a sanctimonious tool. Pick your fights and don't be petty. It's a challenge, I know.

[h3]Still Dual-Wielding and Stacked Like a Building[/h3]
Look, BJ doesn't even like Bolsheviks! My man. For another telling example, Grace's blacksploitation-inspired arc slaps her out of her grief-induced prejudice; she soon calls everyone brothers and sisters. Try to figure that out after watching some regurgitated clips out of context. "Black Woman With Afro Insults White Men!"... Sour-ass lunacy. And her sassy speech on balls was sharp. The two actual low points are the lack of weapon variety and too many unskippable cutscenes. One may guess why it's an issue from the prelude. You know how your dad forces you to shoot your dog at the very start? At this point, few people can bag poor old Bessie faster than me. One positive deviation is that you're forced to play aggressively to excel. Forget leaning or stealth, go oldschool. Terror Billy, still dual-wielding and stacked like a building, is lethal and fast. It pays to outflank your foes, not get bogged down in a camping match. You can surround your enemies with your overwhelming, omnipotent presence to end a fight quickly and hit the Griddy. It's a cathartic way to play! Granted, that change wasn't communicated well, making people question themselves and the game. I learned it from Renn's Reviews, then happily confirmed the theory myself.

I have to be honest on this one, guys. The ending left me feeling underwhelmed and utterly disappointed with this sequel.
It's a shame because I absolutely loved The New Order, and was hoping The New Colossus would continue to impress with the story and gameplay. Unfortunately, The New Colossus only delivers with about half of those aspects, and I will explain to you why.


[h1]Mein Kampf with Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus[/h1]


First, take a serious look at all the ratings and accolades The New Colossus has under the store page. 4.5/5? 9/10? 
"EXTREMELY SATISFYING"?- [b]What effing game did you guys play?[/b] because it's really uneven at times. The biggest problem for me with this game is how repetitive, inconsistent, and how frustrating this game can be after you first arrive in America, I say "frustrating" because of how poor the 'stealth' is, as well as the time it takes for a single Nazi to blow you away from 100 - 0 health in a matter of seconds, with pixel perfect lazer accuracy. I played all the way through on the "Bring 'em on!" difficulty. And on higher difficulties, its absolutely bullshiza, you die almost immediately the second enemies open fire on your @ss, and there are many many Nazis to kill here.

The stealth in this game just... doesn't work most of the time, that's not to say you can't be sneaky at all, but it's extremely difficult to pull off while making your way toward the high value targets. Enemies can spot you even when you aren't clearly visible; it drives mad. The New Order did stealth sections far better than The New Colossus.
And it's appalling to me Machine games/ Bethesda has tied an achievement to the [url=http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1217562418] Mein Leben difficulty[/url] with how broken and difficult this game is. You'd have to complete it without dying, without saving, in a single sitting in a 7-9 hour game, and if you die or the game unexpectedly crashes, you have to start ALL OVER. With how often this game crashes. Good luck.

As for the characters in the main story, the main characters just appear as preset stereotypes: The sassy black chick, The preacher with the mid-western accent, the paranoid conspiracy theorist- none of these new characters have anywhere near the depth of the original characters, which are really the only one's I cared about throughout the story. Especially Fergus and Wyatt.


[h1]Fergus and Wyatt[/h1]

[url=http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1217334314]Fergus Reid[/url] and [url=http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1217333030]Probst Wyatt III[/url]
These are the two characters that stood out most for me while playing through the game. Unfortunately, they both only serve to play as a backseat role for the entirety of the story, and only a very slight change in gameplay. At the beginning, the game wants you to feel like it's the most important choice you'll make that will follow you for the rest of the game (few times it does), but shortly after the first hour, you'll most likely forget you even made that decision because it barely reflects.
Really the only time either of them shine is during the cut-scenes, which I have to admit I love Fergus and Wyatt in these scenes (I'm not gonna spoil them, don't worry), they are funny in several, but later, you can really connect with them, especially Wyatt.

I just wish they had more screen time.





[h1]Where's the revolution?[/h1]

Another problem this game had for me is the fact you never get that revolution feeling. You feel like you're the only one fighting the Nazis most of the time; there's only a handful of people you meet who are seen fighting the Nazis, but you never actually fight alongside them. 
Imagine the emotion Machine Games could have given the players here. Picture you leading resistance fighters into a Nazi base, liberating Americans, raising the flag of the United States of America over the Nazi base with someone playing The Star-Spangled Banner.- none of this happens. It's a missed opportunity to put a great feeling in the player's heart.
 It's a shame to me because look at how they advertised this game, they barely deliver on that aspect of revolution, #NOMORENAZIS, "make America Nazi-free again". The ending left me feeling dissatisfied with high expectations.

[h1]The Positives[/h1]

Now I let it all out and explained the negatives, but does that mean this game is terrible. No. Not at all. There are bright spots in The New Colossus.
- I really like the gun play. Duel wielding shotguns and assault rifles while massacring Nazis is very satisfying.
-The hand to hand takedowns are extremely graphic and awesome
- Halfway through the game, it shocked me with an unexpected event.
- Some scenes in the game, you actually watch in first-person as you witness disturbing events illustrating the ideology of the Nazis,
- The cutscenes are well produced and entertaining to watch. Most of them.
- You learn more about William J. Blazkowicz and his past.
- Killing Nazis.
- Strawberry Milkshakes.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]

My Final Verdict for Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus stands at a 6/10.

Unfortunately for me, the cons of Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus outweigh the pros, so I have to recommend against this game. Is it bad? Like I said. No. I recommend picking this up during a sale if you loved the New Order, but if you haven't, ignore this one and play The New Order first. Only then should you consider Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus.

Alright guys. I hope I could help you out with my review. Think it out before making purchases, Fight for good gaming, and as always, I will see you on the next review.

[b]Back in the '60s[/b]

Released 3 years after its predecessor, [i]The New Order[/i], BJ's story continues right after he rid the world of [i]Deathshead[/i]. Well, this is not entirely true as he undergoes a life-saving operation first  which requires him to recuperate for several months. The prologue immediately sets the tone for the sequel: BJ, now bound to a wheelchair, has to wake up and assist the resistance by fighting off Nazis at their new base of operations which is a submarine this time.

Doing a takedown in our wheelchair is as fun as it gets. We welcome back [i]Frau Engel[/i] who is now joined by her obese daughter (for a short period of time, that is). Instead of Europe the focus will be on America - we visit locales such as Manhattan (this is the area where the atomic bomb was dropped) and look for new tech in Roswell (no, not in Area 51 but in 52!). The creators' favourite film is still [i]Iron Sky[/i] but in order not to repeat themselves we go to Venus instead of the Moon this time.

[b]Familiar game mechanics[/b]

Not much has changed here. Dual wielding is still a good way to kill many enemies in a short period of time. We have some new guns, of course, and collectibles now include looking for upgrades for our guns. The upgrade kit is not for a specific weapon - we decide which one we wish to use it for. I recommend that you add the suppressor to the pistol so that you can make your stealth approach significantly easier.

By playing in a varied way we unlock perks and we can also upgrade these (all come with additional ranks). The difference from the previous episode is that this does not come in the form of a skill tree - you don't have to complete one to unlock another. The system now is way more streamlined. Some items are missing but this is story-related.

[b]Semi-open world approach[/b]

I played this episode almost twice as long as I did its predecessor. This is partly due to the fact that we now have additional DLC campaigns instead of having a separately released expansion title which was [i]Old Blood[/i] in 2015. The second reason for this is the [i]Enigma Machine[/i] introduced by the developers. By eliminating enemy generals we can collect their punch cards (referred to as enigmas). Then using the aforementioned machine on our submarine we can complete a minigame to unlock locations for [i]Übercommanders[/i]. These are generals (a bit stronger, though) whose death cards are part of the many collectibles we have in New Colossus. 

The game basically unlocks the previously completed stages that are once again populated by enemy combatants. There is no story here (no cutscenes); it's all about finding the commanders and looting their dead bodies. Some of the other collectibles we can only find on these levels as some offer new sections we previously didn't have access to. Employing this machine is an interesting concept; not necessarily original but we can always return and do some murdering in order to acquire the highest level of those nasty perks.

[b]Themen und Drama[/b]

I liked the story and the new characters offered by the sequel. Some of them are simply unforgettable: there's Grace who looks like Pam Grier - a very strong African-American leader BJ recruits from their hiding location in the Empire State Building. His partner slash husband, Super Spesh, is a crazy conspiracy-theorist who believes in aliens. The cutscene taking place in his diner in Roswell is one of the best New Colossus has to offer. 

There is more emphasis now on the crew Blazko has as part of the resistance. The main group is still relatively small but there are a lot of others we can talk to at the base and for some reason the creators decided to pick different nationalities here - the crew consist of French, Italians or even Finnish. It's worth listening to their discussions - we might get an extra side mission we have to complete here. I also liked listening to the various accents they have. 

One of the main criticism against the sequel is the nonsense story it has. It has its unrealistic moments while at the same time it tries to be really funny. With Grace and her crew the creators introduced the counterculture of the '60s (hippies!) but I think it is too early to have them here. Also, enemies now include dogs shooting lasers from their eyes (simply called [i]Laserhund[/i]) or the [i]ÜberSoldat[/i] that looks similar to a T-800 robot from the Terminator franchise. Only several months have passed, yet, it is as if technology advanced by a decade or two at least. But hey: you can take down Arnold with just a press of a button! How cool is that?

There is a lot of cutscenes showing Blazko's past; the time he spent with his abusive father while growing up in Texas. His dad, Rip, is given voice acting by [i]Glenn Morshower[/i] - he is a regular when it comes to roles of senators, colonels or other high-ranking officials in US blockbuster films. Fans of Battlefield 3 will immediately recognise his voice. The voice acting for Hitler (no, not a spoiler, he was in the trailers) is also top-notch!

[b]Zusammenfassung[/b]

I had fun with the next instalment of the new Wolfeinstein franchise concocted by [i]MachineGames[/i]. There's no multiplayer, no coop just pure single-player fun with lots of shootouts all taking place in a retrofuturistic era. It has great characters and a solid story (minus some of the nonsense technological approaches) and proves that it's still a great pastime using those machine guns in dual-wielding mode.

Wolfenstein: The Collosal Disappointment.

-Nearly 70% of the game consists of cutscenes. I'm not joking, there are 4 hours of them, and the game took me about 7 hours to beat. Some of the cutscenes are great, but that doesn't change the fact that you're spending most of the game not actually playing it.

-The new characters are poorly developed and are actively infuriating.

-The villain has nearly no screentime and is barely relevant to the plot. Deathshead in Wolfenstein TNO only appeared in person a couple of times, but his prescense was EVERYWHERE, and you really felt B.J's hatred and resentment of him. Frau Engel just cannot compare. Even her portrayal in the first game was better. There is only one secondary antagonist, instead of the varied cast of TNO. 

-The level design is mediocre and reeks of wasted potential. Bethesda has the whole Nazi-occupied America to work with, and they chose to put B.J in grey corridors, bombed out buildings, and warehouses. Most of the levels in Wolfenstein II could easily be put into any other FPS. Most insulting of all, you get to see Nazi-occupied Roswell, with KKK members and Nazis roaming the streets. Think you get to mow down a Klan rally or tear up the streets of New Mexico? Nope, only in the very boring and stale side missions that were added as filler content and have no plot relevance.

-Speaking of the side missions: in place of a propery "Replay Mission" feature, the developers let you replay certain sections of certain levels that have been cut to about a 3 minute length and have almost no story. And to play those watered down sections, you need to first solve tedious puzzles that require you to literally farm Commander enemies for an item that lets you access the puzzles. Fail the puzzle, and you lose cards. Your reward for beating all of the levels? Nothing.

-The pace of the game is blistering despite the cutscenes interrupting gameplay every 5 minutes. You almost never get any worldbuilding or breather levels. Just nonstop shooting, which becomes exhausting eventually. TNO had nearly perfect pacing, each encounter felt well-designed and came at just the right moment. 

-Enemy variety pales in comparison to TNO. In TNO, you had massive Super Soldiers, Rocket-firing soldiers, giant Robots, attack dogs, dual-wielding shrapnel-firing shotgunners, drones and more. In The New Collusus, dogs and drones almost never appear, and super soldiers have been turned from legitimately threatening mini-bosses to buffoons with paper-mache armor. The only remotely new enemy is a human-size robot that is even less of a threat than other enemies due to their extremely low health and damage.

-Weapon variety is atrocious. You have a pistol, an smg, an assault rifle, a shotgun, a laser gun (not as fun as it sounds), a weird grenade pistol that has almost no ammunition, and a few heavy weapons that drop from the Super Soldiers. TNO had a similar roster of weapons, but this is the sequel. There should be more weapons, not the same. In TNO, most of the weapons had alternate modes that changed how the weapon works. For example, the Assault Rifle could be changed into a Rocket Launcher, the Shotgun could be changed to shoot shrapnel pellets that bounce everywhere, and the Marksman Rifle could be changed into a laser-powered assault rifle. Here, each modification is now a straight upgrade instead of something you can toggle, taking more options away from the player. 

-The Laserkraftwerk has been especially butchered. In TNO, you found upgrades throughout the game that made it more powerful. It was easily the most iconic weapon in the game, and had a secondary mode that let you cut through obstacles and opened up new routes for those who are patient. Not only was it a powerful weapon, but a powerful tool that could be used in a variety of ways. In TNC, the cutting mode is gone, and there are only three upgrades that barely change the way it works. It is barely recognizable from the original and looks like a shotgun with a tape recorder attached to it instead of the big, badass, powerful laser cannon of doom that it once was.


-The soundtrack is unremarkable and in some cases unfitting for what is going on. Nowhere near as iconic as the DOOM soundtrack.

-The game ends at the point where the second half should have began. No final boss fight, no buildup. You just press a button and the game ends. To make things worse, the final cutscene is the most obvious sequel-bait I've ever seen, in contrast to the ending of TNO which nicely concluded the game while still leaving the possibility of a sequel.

I cannot in good faith Recommend Wolfenstein II. Bethesda blew it, let's hope that DOOM II doesn't suffer the same fate.

It is hard for me to believe that the same developer that made the excellent games Wolfenstein: The New Order and Wolfenstein: The Old Blood also made this. Wolfenstein II has a beautiful new graphics engine and greatly improved loading times. Everything else is weak.

Cutscenes are too frequent and too long. All of the new characters are annoying, and the cutscenes are much more about them than you. We hear about America being oppressed, but rarely see evidence of it. The New Order made your blood boil through skillful exposition of events, often while you actually had control of your character, and the urge to kill Nazis was real. Does Wolfenstein II even have Nazis? After countless battles against mecha-soldiers, flying laser drones, and cyberdogs, I thought I was just fighting somebody’s robot army.

Stealth is far less viable; I rarely bothered with it. The alternating “now you’re stealthy, now you’re out with guns blazing” style was a distinguishing feature of the first game and created many tense, emergent moments. It is sad to see this balance lost here in the sequel.

There isn’t enough feedback on damage being dealt or received. Fine aiming for things like headshots is not rewarding (everything is a robot; see above). In contrast to the crazy futuristic tech all around you, your arsenal is disappointingly basic. The different weapons struggle to find a niche as well. The Sturmgewehr (assault rifle) with the scope and armor-piercing upgrades is universally strong, and its ammo is plentiful.

There are occasional spurts of fun gunplay to be found throughout the game’s relatively simplistic levels. But then you’ll hit a button prompt to exit an area and lurch into an embarrassing display of awfully written, cringeworthy dialog. There aren’t even any boss fights. What happened here?

I approached Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus with the same mindset I had for the first game. I wanted to evaluate it based on structure, gameplay systems, narrative consistency and technical execution, not just atmosphere.

The first major issue for me is length. I finished the game in roughly 10 hours. That is noticeably shorter than The New Order, and it reinforces a pattern in this series. The experience feels condensed, almost rushed. It is not about wanting a 200-hour grind. It is about narrative consistency and world development. The game moves forward quickly, delivers cutscenes, pushes combat encounters, and then it ends.

The core problem remains the same as in the first game. Enemy AI has not significantly improved. Stealth is still basic. Difficulty settings once again mainly increase enemy health and damage output instead of improving tactical behavior. Even on the highest difficulty, it often feels like playing on normal, except bosses become damage sponges. The challenge comes from inflated health pools rather than smarter combat design.

On top of that, achievement tracking is inconsistent. I unlocked achievements at moments that did not correspond to what I was actually doing in-game, which suggests tracking issues.

Technically, performance is improved compared to the first game. The engine feels more stable and responsive. Combat remains satisfying. Weapons feel impactful. The moment-to-moment gameplay is still solid and aggressive.

However, the narrative execution feels limited in scope. The premise is strong, but the story does not expand the world in a meaningful way. What is happening in the rest of the world? Are there other resistance movements globally? How does the larger geopolitical situation evolve? These elements are barely explored. The game focuses heavily on linear progression instead of expanding its universe.

It feels like a Doom-style structure placed into a Nazi alternate-history setting. The combat design clearly prioritizes speed, aggression and spectacle. That is not inherently negative, but for a player who values story depth, worldbuilding and continuity, it feels underdeveloped. The series has the potential to combine strong gameplay with a more ambitious narrative structure, including side missions that support the main arc, broader resistance networks, and a more cohesive evolution of the revolutionary group. Instead, progression often feels segmented between games rather than organically continuous.

The game is not bad. It is competently made, visually strong, mechanically functional and thematically consistent. But it does not innovate. It does not significantly evolve the formula. The protagonist still feels almost invulnerable, a near-Terminator figure carrying the weight of the entire world alone. The story, while dramatic, follows a fairly familiar hero narrative structure.

I would place Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus between 6 and 7. It is a good game. It is functional, entertaining and technically solid. But it does not revolutionize its genre, it does not meaningfully evolve its systems, and it does not expand its world to the degree its premise deserves.

Final Addition to the Review

To clarify something important: this is not a case of “I didn’t like the game.” I did enjoy it. The combat is solid, the production value is high, and the theme is strong. The issue is not quality. The issue is ambition.

When you build a game around such a powerful premise an alternate world dominated by Nazis you have the opportunity to create something structurally unique. Not just aesthetically different, but mechanically and narratively distinctive. Instead, the core gameplay loop remains conventional: run, shoot, cutscene, repeat. The theme is bold, but the design philosophy is safe.

Recycling ideas is not a problem. Every game builds on what came before. But if you recycle, you need to evolve. You need to add identity. You need to refine, expand, or innovate. Simply applying a different setting over an already established formula does not make something truly new.

Wolfenstein II does not fail because it is bad. It falls short because it could have been more. With its concept, it had the foundation to expand its world, deepen its systems, and establish a stronger mechanical identity. Instead, it chooses familiarity over evolution.

Game development progresses through iteration, but meaningful iteration requires improvement, not replication.

Its over the top characters and exaggerated stereotypes are still there, but I guess this time they offended people because they're american stereotypes this go around.  The new characters are enjoyable enough, though we don't really get to learn much about them. Unlike the first game where you'll have plenty of time to learn about each of the cast members, the resistance has gotten so large and you don't really get to work with any of the characters closely.  It's kind of a shame too, even fergus/wyatt don't really get much screentime. The only new character who gets a lot of exposure is grace, but she's kind of annoying and one-dimensional.

Let's talk a bit about [b]stage design[/b].   It's definitely not as varied as the first game, where almost every stage is a new location. There's only a handful of locations in the second game. Airship, Manhatten, Roswell,  New orleans, Venus.  There are also a few of very small stages, courthouse, Roswell (town) and a Texas farm.  The manhatten levels suck. It's the ruins of a nuked city, filled with grey everywhere, and a subway section. New orleans suffers from almost the same problem, it's dark and run down, or you're in the sewers. It's a bland level with little that says louisana or new orleans. The roswell levels are pretty solid, it feels like the most work went into them. There are usually multiple angles of approach and you get to sneak through a nazi base.  None of the levels are memorable as the broken bridge, prison camp, moonbase, or even the london museum raid from the first game.


[h1]Enemy Variety and Weapons[/h1]

The different kinds of enemies are almost unchanged from the first game, and they're all pretty bland. The new supersoldiers are no longer absurd bullet sponges, in exchange for being able to thrust across the map. There's a new kind of laser dog thing, and the Super Nazi Robot, that you fight as a boss in the first game comes back as a recurring enemy with different weapons. That's about it.  The kampfhunds are more annoying than ever, and I'll bring that up later.

To compound the problem with the low number of enemies, the number of weapons is virtually unchanged from the first game. There's an SMG now, and a sort of pistol grenade launcher I never bothered with.  For some reason the heavy MG was removed, and there are instead 4 heavy weapons instead. One doesn't appear until almost the end of the game, and the others are kind of useless on the harder difficulties. The heavy shotgun weapon is terrible. There's already only a few weapons in the game, so they're all different and useful, right? 
No.  If you're sneaking you'll use the pistol. 
If you aren't you'll dual wield the assault rifle.

Fully upgraded it will fire single shots fairly accurately and be able to kill pretty every kind of enemy with ease, aside from the large panzerhunds. Even then, it will only take a single reload if you aren't hitting any weakpoints. The assault rifle reloads quickly, is ammo efficient, is effective at every range, and ammunition for it is plentiful. 

About halfway through the game you get access to gadgets which can offer new ways to get through a level. Each gadget also gives you a few passive bonus skills. Unfortunately aside from 1 of them (the extendo boots) they're mostly useless outside of acting like glorified keycards.

[h1]Sound Design[/h1]

With the game set int 1950/60's america, I thought it would have at least a few time relevant comtemporary hits, but I guess this is kind of subverted with the whole being conquered by germany situation. The music that is left is kind of bland, but nothing offensive.  What's really offensive is that just like the first game it's often hard to hear what the characters are saying, it being BJ's monologues during the levels or even characters speaking at the home base. Enemies are abnormally quiet. Despite them all wearing boots and armor, only the supersoldiers and giant robots will make any sort of noise while moving, no matter how close, no matter the surface. For a game with stealth aspects, this is kind of unexcusable. The biggest insult are the stealth (aka all of them) kampfhunds; They don't bark, they don't growl, you can't hear them running. Your only audio notice to them is that they make a wimpy growl noise as they lunge at you. A fast enemy that can knock you over, and is small enough to be hidden even when running because of chest high cover everywhere that gives no warning of its presence is just bad game design. The only thing from keeping it getting out of hand is that they're a pretty rare enemy.

[h1]Other[/h1]
I beat the game on the highest difficulty available at the start.  I wouldn't reccomend it. It's kind of a crapshoot as an enemy firing at you might miss, or it might take about 80% of your life in a short window.   The difficulty right below that probably offers the best balance between challenge and fun.

The ending is 100% buy the sequel. It wasn't particularly offensive to me, but I say the same thing about Mankind Divided's ending.

The game's length is inflated with [optional] asssination missions, which have you return to stages you've already cleared to fight enemies again and explore usually a single new room in the level and kill a generic commander. 


[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Despite all these bad things said about the game, it's still a fairly competant FPS game, but it's definitely carried more along by it's style, setting, and characters, not its gameplay.

Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is the sequel to the absolutely amazing The New Order, but this sequel is a slight disappointment.

Story:

Wolfenstein II begins as soon as the first game ends, to show that BJ has survived, but his severe injuries have put him into a coma after he comes to, he finds himself bound to a wheelchair and the base he's stored on attacked by nazis. After fighting them off, BJ learns that he will die soon, so he needs to recruit new members for the resistance.

The story for this game is rather bland. Just like the The New Order , Wolfenstein II has some absolutely crazy moments and some great new characters, that are a parody on the 60s Blaxploitation genre. But unlike the first game, The New Colossus can't find a nice pace for the story and a lot of the sections become sort of out of place. The first half of the game is insanely serious, with some deep emotional story pieces, not to mention some disturbing sequences and the second half is balls to the wall crazy with lighthearted fun and basically no emotion. I feel like they should have found a better mix of the two.

Graphics:

Wolfenstein II looks amazing. It's really impressive how good the graphics are, especially in the later sections of the game, like exploring a nuked New York city, New Orleans and a KKK and Nazi overrun city.  I really enjoyed the graphics and in my opinion it looks way better than the first game.

Audio:

The voice acting is absolutely top notch and I think every character has done an absolutely amazing job. The soundtrack composed by DOOM (2016) and Prey (2017) Mick Gordon is good, but it's not as memorable as DOOM 2016s soundtrack was. It's definitely not bad by any means and has some good music that makes blasting away Nazis is super fun. 

Gameplay:

This is where I have to say the game is a rather mixed bag. The gunplay is as satisfying as ever. Gunning down Nazis is so much fun and just ripping them apart with powerful weaponry and your trusty axes has never felt better, but the biggest problem is the level and design and the games attempt at artificial difficulty  with throwing generals every encounter.

The games level design in the sequel is a lot more open ended having a lot of open areas where the levels elevate, so for example there is section where you fight in an abandoned apartment that has multiple floors to go through and this becomes rather annoying as enemies hide themselves in some weird locations and not to mention the generals. The game throws two generals every other gun fight and if you are spotted they will call in reinforcements and with the games level design finding them is often a pain.

The stealth is good, but the elevated level design doesn't really help stealth being fluid. most enemies are placed in locations that they will notice you as soon as you are even in the range of their view and once a single enemy spots you, everyone on the map knows where you are. The best way to play this game is to take out generals while in stealth and then go loud which is what I started doing after the first few levels.

Also the game is short, way shorter than the first game. It took me around 6 hours to finish the story on the hard difficulty and the DLC extended the play time to 10 hours, meanwhile the first game took me roughly around 8 hours to finish and The Old Blood took me around 7 hours which was cheap spin off, not to mention The New Colossus is 50% gameplay 50% cutscenes.

Verdict:

I wish there was a neutral option, cause I don't think this game is bad, but I don't think this game is nowhere near as good as the first game or even it's prequel. However on a sale I'd say go for it, but as it is, just go play the first game and then spin off. 

Final Rating:
6/10

+ Gameplay is a lot fun
+ Soundtrack is good

Cons:
- Story is inconsistent in tone
- Level design is atrocious

[i]Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus[/i] is a worthy sequel to 2014's terrific first-person shooter (FPS) [i]Wolfenstein: The New Order[/i]. Once more, we're presented with a story-heavy FPS that doesn't just consist of a string of shooting sequences like 2015's prequel [i]Wolfenstein: The Old Blood[/i], but with heart, charm and character to enrich the experience. 

As far as the action is concerned, a lot of people have said it and it's hard to explain why exactly, but it genuinely feels very satisfying to kill nazis and their robotic constructions in these games. If you're into FPS at all, you owe it to yourself to play [i]The New Colossus[/i], but I strongly advise you play [i]The New Order[/i] first because story-wise, [i]The New Colossus[/i] is a true sequel.

Note: this game requires almost 50GB of disk space! This is just for the base game, without the DLC. I'm not interested in the DLC as people agree it adds nothing of value to the experience, and all of the DLC have 'mostly negative' reviews.


[h1]Story[/h1]

The modern Wolfenstein games are set in an alternate history related to World War 2 in which the nazis weren't defeated by the allied forces in 1944. The nazis won the conflict due to their amazing technological advancements. Although the nazis have been dealt a serious blow during the events of [i]Wolfenstein: The New Order[/i], they are far from conquered. 

On the contrary, they have established a firm grip on the USA. The secondary antagonist of the first game, Irene Engel, is the main antagonist this time. The protagonist is again B.J. Blazkowicz, prominent member of the Resistance. Your task this time, besides killing a thousand or so nazis who'll stand in your way to achieve your goals, is to stop general Engel and to start the second American Revolution. Yet again, this Wolfenstein game will take you to a variety of locations. If you thought the moon base in [i]Wolfenstein: The New Order[/i] would be pretty much as far as a Wolfenstein game would ever take you, you're in for a surprise…


[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

This is one of those games that gets it right, although it's hard to describe what 'it' is. 

The shooting mechanics are pure, genuine fun. You'll be able to use a small arsenal of weapons, including suppressed pistols for silent kills (so as not to alert all of the surrounding nazis), shotguns for your short-range killing needs, scoped rifles for long-distance precision killing, grenade-launching pistols (yes, really) and even laser cannons.

Most weapons can be dual-wielded, which makes you feel like an even more radical killing machine but it burns through ammo faster. Also, most weapons can be upgraded by finding upgrade kits scattered throughout the game world. I like the fact that you can freely choose which weapon to upgrade and what upgrade to apply every time you find a kit, as opposed to having to wait until you reach the place where that one upgrade you'd like is finally found.

Going in guns blazing is not always the best idea, especially on higher difficulties. You'll want to sneak your way towards the nazi commanders first and kill them silently so they can't sound the alarm and call for reinforcements. You may also want to silently eliminate as much nazis as you can, by using silent weapons like a throwing axe or a suppressed pistol, or by performing a melee takedown on them. Playing like this creates a satisfying tension and a rush when things go right. And if things go wrong, you reload and try again, using the knowledge you gathered from previous attempts.

Like in the other modern Wolfenstein games, B.J. has a list of perks to unlock, which make him an even more efficient killing machine. For example, killing a certain number of enemies while dual-wielding increases your ammo capacity, or sneakily killing nazi commanders increases the time it takes them to sound the alarm when they see you. Each of the 18 perks really add value to your character's abilities, so they're definitely something to go for. You can actually 'farm' these perks because their count carries over if you reload a saved game.

In between hostile areas where action is key, you return to your base, which is a submarine this time. Here, you can interact with NPCs who may give you a side quest or just offer a bit of banter. In the helm of the submarine, you'll find an Enigma machine. By means of a minigame, the Enigma machine allows you to unlock the position of nazi commanders who've moved into areas you've cleared before. You can then return to these areas and you'll find them full of new enemies and collectibles. This is a nice way to add optional content to the game.

After finishing the main quest, you're returned to your base and you can wrap up sidequests and complete the collectibles and perks for their respective achievements.


[h1]Graphics and sound[/h1]

[i]Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus[/i]'s graphics are fine. They aren't the most photorealistic but they're definitely nice enough to make you want to take some screenshots from time to time, if that's your thing. Color banding was often noticeable to the point of annoying, but that issue may be due to my hardware or settings.

The music is simply fantastic. While exploring or sneaking around, the score is very atmospheric and it adds palpable tension. During combat or other action sequences, you're treated to raw industrial metal beats that get your adrenaline pumping.

As for the voice acting, I can't be too generous with my wording. This game has top-notch voice acting, both for the main characters and for the nameless nazis who shout battle cries and instructions in German while you're laying waste to them.


[h1]On Steam's extra features[/h1]

[i]Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus[/i] has no Steam Trading Cards. 

Of the 80 Steam Achievements, only 50 are related to the main game. The DLC isn't worth buying (it has a 'mostly negative' rating), which means 37.5% of the achievements will remain incomplete forever if you only buy the main game. I'm not an obsessive completionist, but still I think that's a bit of a shame. Achievements for DLC should only be set as a target if you actually own the DLC.

Achieving even 62.5% completion, the maximum for the main game, is not an easy feat because of two reasons. First and foremost, there is an achievement for each of the difficulty modes. The 'very hard' and 'ultra hard' modes are very challenging, but the special 'Mein Leben' difficulty means going through the game without saving and with only one life, so perma-death if you will. Nothing is impossible, but not being allowed to make a single mistake is a very unforgiving requirement for a long and challenging game like this, so hats off to anyone who legitimately achieved this one!

Secondly, there's a very grindy achievement i.e. collect 1,000 nazi helmets in one game. As there's no tracker for this achievement, it's impossible to say how many helmets you have collected by playing through the game but people estimate it at 250 to 350. So you need to find a place where there are a couple of helmets lying around, save, pick up the helmets, reload, and repeat that a couple of hundreds of times. Not my idea of a fun or challenging achievement.

Apart from 11 story-related achievements, there is a nice variety of achievements awarded for performing optional tasks, for maxing all of the perks, for finding all of the collectibles, and stuff like that. This bunch of achievements is fun to do, and they add some additional optional challenges to the game.

Each new Wolfenstein game does something better than the other: The New Order has the best writing, the Old Blood has the best aesthetics, whereas The New Colossus... well, it's hard to say.
It's definitely not the story and characters. They are the complete opposite - the writing is just awful. The characters are not memorable at all and they are written like caricatures, like jokes and I simply don't care about them and their fates.
The story does have a few dark scenes, but the majority of them do not have an impact as they either have absolutely ridiculous premises or are followed by a tone deaf joke. 

The gunplay, however, combined with the gore system and execution animations, are one of the most satisfying I've experienced in any shooter. It's endlessly fun dual-wielding shotguns, mini grenade launchers and 2 weapons from different classes, like a pistol and the machine gun, which wasn't present in previous 2 games. Coming back to the execution animations - whoever came up with the idea to have the tomahawk as the melee weapon is a genius. Not only are the animations so brutal, especially when combined with excellent sound design, the ability to throw them and see enemies get their limb cut off from a distance is just addictingly fun. You are also given a choice to select one of 3 abilities that will help you in combat and help you discover hidden secrets and collectibles in the world. This is also a great way to encourage replayability, as some of these secrets require the other 2 abilities, which you can unlock when replaying missions. 

The level design is once again fantastic. Not only that, but the entire art style and graphics are breathtaking. You can stop every few steps to just look around and take screenshots.
Another neat addition that I really enjoyed is having the entire character model rendered in real time, even if it's a first-person shooter. Looking down and seeing your character actually reacting to the world and not just seeing floating hands is not something you see a lot in FPS games.

Another issue I have with this game, not just writing, is the stealth system. On the surface it's almost identical to the previous 2 games - avoid getting seen by the enemies, use silent weapons or melee, take out the commander as soon as you can. However, now, if you get seen by a single enemy, tens of meters away from the commander, the entire section will get alerted and enemies will keep spawning in waves unless you eliminate all present commanders. Which is a bit ridiculous. At times it seems that the guns-blazin approach is the only correct one, as some of these stealth sections take waaay to much time and patience, only to be wasted by some BS enemy seeing you from across the map.

There's not much to say about the expansions - it's more Wolfenstein 2 missions but you're playing as different characters, each having one of the 3 abilities from the main game. There are no new weapons, no new enemies and no new bosses. So get them if you are craving more singleplayer action.

Mick Gordon has done it again - the soundtrack is a blessing as always. It works so well with this game's themes, adds necessary seasoning during combat and offers peace during cutscenes, especially in more heartwarming moments. 

All in all - highly recommend for the combat and music alone. Do not go playing this game expecting a masterpiece in terms of the dialogue, the characters, the story making sense, well-thought out stealth sections, but expect brutal combat, satisfying weapons, gorgeous graphics, great level design and over the top action.

Wolfenstein 2: New Colossus is the sequel to New Order, the first person shooter set in an alternate timeline where the Nazis won World War 2. The year is now 1961 and player character BJ Blazkowicz is trying to grow the resistance and liberate the world, starting in America.

New Order was an amazing game. It came very close to winning my 2014 Game of the Year award, and its either first or second on my list of best FPSes of all time, depending on my mood (Doom 2016 has better combat, but New Order is the better all around game because of its superior story). New Colossus can’t quite match that level of awesome, but its still a very good game.

I have to say that I think the community has judged New Colossus very unfairly. I’ve seen the 69% “mixed” Steam rating, and I’ve scrolled through a bunch of the all time most helpful reviews, which are almost all negative, and I’m really confused. I feel like I’ve somehow played a different game to everybody else, because I’ve enjoyed most of my time in New Colossus, especially from a gameplay point of view.

The good

-	The shooting mechanics feel perfect, especially with a mouse.
-	Dual wield any weapon, or any combination of weapons. One of my favourite setups was an assault rifle in my right hand to kill enemies at range, and an automatic shotgun in my left hand in case somebody got up in my face. You can also use a pistol, SMG, laser rifle, and grenade/rocket launcher.
-	You know how most shooters will only give you the most powerful weapons a few times over the whole campaign? Well in New Colossus, you’ll find heavy weapons in almost every fight, either dropped by enemies or ripped from turret stands. I absolutely love the way the laser cannon just melts Nazi flesh, causing them to evaporate into a puff of smoke. The flamethrower is pretty toasty too :) Wandering around the level, racking up a massive kill count with these weapons really made me feel like Terror-Billy, the unstoppable death machine who gives the Nazis nightmares.
-	There’s a decent variety of enemies, including machinegunners, shotgunners, dogs, heavies, laser robots, flying droids, fire breathing robot dogs, and massive rocket spamming robots.
-	Sneak up behind enemies and perform melee kills. Stealth kill commanders to stop them calling for reinforcements. Although to be honest, the combat was so much fun that at times I wasn't really trying too hard to be stealthy, because I actually wanted them to give me more guys to shoot.
-	Level up perks to gain passive buffs. Examples include getting dual wield kills to increase maximum ammo capacity, and making kills while health is overcharged to slow the speed that overcharge fades.
-	Enemy AI is pretty good. They managed to flank me on several occasions.
-	It took me 13.5 hours to finish the campaign. This includes time spent in optional side missions which are unlocked through a code cracking minigame, where the objective is to kill a high ranking Nazi commander.
-	Flawless technical performance. I had a solid 60 fps with most settings maxed at 1080p, no stuttering, no bugs, no crashes. Keys are fully rebindable.

The bad

Unfortunately, [i]Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus[/i] isn't the blindside reboot that its predecessor [i]Wolfenstein: The New Order[/i] is, nor the love letter to retro gaming that prequel [i]Wolfenstein: The Old Blood[/i] is. It's the beginning of a downward trend that continued in [i]Youngblood[/i], but [i]New Colossus[/i] still has high points that outnumber its low points.  To dig into why I'm only mildly positive on this title, let's examine [i]New Colossus[/i] as a sequel to [i]New Order[/i], as a work of exploitation fiction, and as a work of earnest political commentary.

[h1][i]New Colossus[/i] as a sequel to [i]New Order[/i][/h1]
On the face of it, [i]New Colossus[/i] excels as a sequel, albeit it's a 'more of what you love' kind of sequel. In his endless battle against the Nazis of this dystopian alternate timeline, protagonist William "BJ" Blazkowicz uses the exact same arsenal of weapons he used in [i]New Order[/i] and [i]Old Blood[/i] to fight the exact same roster of enemies that he fought in [i]New Order[/i] and [i]Old Blood[/i], albeit both BJ and the enemies are equipped with a few minor new gimmicks to shake things up a little. The wheel is not reinvented here: instead, MachineGames really focuses on what makes a Wolfenstein-Reboot combat encounter work, and they've polished the retro-corridor-shooter game loop of their franchise to a spit-shine here. Compared to combat encounters in the prior two games, encounters here are more varied, shooting galleries flow better, and the fights are both more fun and more challenging (with those two often informing each other).

However, I'd mentioned that the game is a "retro corridor shooter," like the entire franchise before it, and that belies one of its greatest problems: level diversity. You see, the plot of the game concerns BJ returning to an occupied America to help liberate it from the Nazi oppressors, but for the sake of the gameplay loop, this America -- one of the largest nations on Earth, with incredible open spaces and biome diversity -- needs to be an America comprised exclusively of corridors.  Therefore, the game fails to fully explore what a post-nuclear Manhattan wasteland looks like, because the Manhattan levels are spent in the corridors of its subway system. The game fails to explore what a Nazi-occupied New Mexico looks like, because after five minutes of walking a single city block of Roswell, BJ must descend into a military base to shoot through [b]those corridors.[/b] A guerrilla uprising in New Orleans is perceived near-entirely from -- you guessed it -- the corridors of its sewer system.  For a sequel that promised extremely evocative, [i]Man in the High Castle[/i]-esque imagery of a Nazi-occupied America, the game actually has very few artistically memorable combat arenas.

[i]Doom[/i] could get away with this because its Mars base setting is simply a convenient location for video game violence to occur, but it's a weird match for this [i]Wolfenstein[/i] reboot-sequel, which clearly has cinematic aspirations.

[h1][i]New Colossus[/i] as a Grindhouse Movie[/h1]
...Which brings us nicely into the weird push-and-pull at the core of this sequel, which seems to demand to be taken seriously as a commentary on fascism and white supremacy, while also being a very intentional homage to grindhouse cinema.

To be clear, all of the MachineGames [i]Wolfensteins[/i] aspire to be exploitation fiction. [i]Wolfenstein: the New Order[/i] owes a great debt to Tarantino's [i]Inglorious Basterds[/i] and classic works of Nazi exploitation like [i]Ilsa: She-Wolf of the SS[/i]: movies that make titillation of the violence of the Nazi regime. [i]Old Blood[/i] embraced the 1930s serial mood, placing itself squarely in the canon of contemporary Nazi-fightin' genre tributes like [i]Hellboy[/i] and [i]Indiana Jones[/i].  By contrast, this game's 1960s counterculture setting -- albeit an alt-history one that pits iconic American counterculture figures like the Black Panthers and Hippies against the Nazis -- pulls liberally from the canon of blaxploitation, drugsploitation, sexploitation, and more, and these aren't all easy marriages with the Nazi-exploitation genre that the prior two games embodied.

It's hard to articulate, but [i]The New Colossus[/i] is the first game in the series to feel [i]sleazy[/i], in a way that MachineGames was clearly deliberately shooting for but which sometimes steps over the boundaries of good taste in a way that feels edgy for edginess' sake.  Be it black panthers shooting Nazis while crowing about these jive-ass Nazi crackers, or a recurring subplot about how pregnancy hormones are causing BJ's wife Anya to experience sexual pleasure when she shoots Nazis (ultimately culminating in a [i]Shoot Em' Up[/i] style sex-scene-that-is-also-a-gunfight where she multiple-orgasms after pulping seven men with a grenade) the tone of the story feels gratuitous in a way that dulls, rather than sharpens, the edge of its commentary.

[h1][i]New Colossus[/i] as a Work of Commentary[/h1]
This is a problem because [i]Wolfenstein[/i] doesn't exist in a cultural vacuum, especially not [i]New Colossus[/i].  Let's not mince words about it: [i]New Colossus[/i] is the first post-Charlottesville [i]Wolfenstein[/i] title, and the game's marketers played that for everything it was worth to draw deliberate parallels between its in-game sci-fi Nazis and the ugly, resurgent, and suddenly mainstream American white nationalist movement. [i]Wolfenstein: The New Colossus[/i] intentionally inserted itself in a national dialogue, knowing that like Keurig and Nike before them, they could poke the nest of the very worst Americans by making a big dumb show about this game being about Strong Black People Killing Whitey. Predictably, the most fragile egos on the internet came screaming and blubbering to give the game months of free publicity.

I'm, of course, burying the lede here: the obvious question that follows is "so, it's a work of political commentary, right?"

The answer is that no, it really isn't. The most revolutionary that [i]New Colossus[/i] ever gets is tepidly pointing out that white and especially German-descended Americans actually broadly supported the Nazis and that resistance against fascist regimes has always historically come first from communists and minorities, which the game milks for cheap horror; in the Roswell level that is our only encounter with "ordinary" white Americans, they are mewling Nazi toadies, given no characterization beyond "abominably racist."

It's commentary, certainly, but it's facile commentary, and sits poorly with the fact that the story also demands that we see the liberation of these cartoonish bigots as laudable, or even something that they'd want. The finale, where our multiracial, communist hero team go on television and wake up America with a rousing call-to-action, feels unearned because we have seen only bigotry and ugliness, not an America that desires or deserves to be liberated.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
[i]The New Colossus[/i] is the [i]Wolfenstein[/i] for our times: a big, bombastic, flashy work of genre fiction that often threatens to have a point beyond just being rip-roaring violent fun, but which then trips over its own dick trying to make it. [i]New Colossus[/i] enjoys a much-debated spot in the contemporary Gamer Culture Wars that it absolutely is neither good nor [b]bad[/b] enough to deserve. At once ambitious and complacent, filmic and gamey, too political but yet [b]not[/b] political, it defines the "mid," 7/10 first-person shooter.  A good on-sale title.

While I understand the many negatives people have pointed out over the last month, I believe we can see some solid work here. Yes, the cutscenes are excessively long and they do not portray the characters as well as in the first game, but still, most of the shocking and satisfying moments of the game happen in them. It's a very old-school approach to storytelling. I really don't think the proportion of cutscenes to gameplay is 1:1 as it's more like 1:4, especially on higher difficulties which are exceedingly brutal to the player. It may seem though as if the game is constantly interrupting you in your Nazi killing flow, whether it is a cutscene or a pointless postcard from a soldier to his mother. The texts generally don't feel very thought-out and do not shed much light on the world's historical background, like in the first game. 

What I mean by solid work is how well done is the absurdity, insanity and grotesqueness of the current world order and its main players. Frau Engel is one of the most ludicrous and monstrous villains I have ever met. The game throws at you one wow moment after another and the violence and horror are over the top most of the time. The whole part with Hitler is phenomenally well-done as it captures him in both terrifying and comical light. Swastikas are stamped on literally everything you can think of and the game doesn't know the term censorship unless you are playing the German release. There are many new characters, but you still have to have at least a rudimentary knowledge of The New Order in order to better understand the character development. Sigrun, the daughter of Frau Engel, is by far the most interesting one but isn't given much space until the last part of the game. Grace is a swearing machine and deserves a slap.

The gunplay is somewhat insipid when compared to the first game, as the guns feel weak and their sounds don't have the right impact (apart from the laser, which is brilliant). You can now dual-wield any two weapons in your arsenal. I found switching weapons to be painfully slow, plus the models have their FOV far too large and they cover most of the screen, making non-combat situations a bit clunky. The enemies on higher difficulties can now kill you with a few shots, which makes the newly added quicksave button an absolute necessity as you'll probably die way too many times. I don't like that your armour or superbody takes as many shots to fail as a regular Nazi soldier. You'll use Overcharging way more often than in the first game. The excellent automatic cover system from the first game was replaced with a manual one and you have to press Alt + WASD to lean from a cover, which is very clumsy and I honestly didn't use it much.

The game performed very well in the departments of graphics, optimization and various PC-specific settings. However, I had to fix like 5 things before being able to play and still there were many crashes, especially when using the Steam Overlay. The release was flawed with a lot of people experiencing graphical glitches, crashes or they were not able to play the game at all. But much of that was fixed and there are still many fixes about to come as the DLC unlocks over time.

It was a solid experience and I liked it, even though it is not that fresh and awe-inspiring as The New Order.

Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is pure fun. It’s a classic sequel—it takes all the best parts of the previous game and multiplies them by two, or maybe even ten! It’s still the same bone-crushing, blood-soaked shooter, but it doesn’t trap the player in the rigid confines of excessive difficulty. You’re constantly armed with deadly weapons that help you spectacularly rid the game world of Nazis. The villains themselves are caricatures and quite amusing. The plot doesn’t stray far from the first game and follows its same trends. If you want to make a smart investment in some bloody home entertainment, choosing this game is more than justified.

honestly I'm not sure why so many people are having issues with game performance, I've been playing for about 30 hours and haven't encountered anything of the sort. anyways:

PROS:

+it looks gorgeous

+the gunplay kicks ass, the weapons are varied and everything feels satisfying to use

+story is cool, it seems like a lot more thought went into it than in the last game and a few of the story beats will really blow your mind

+surprisingly a lot of replay value, I bet some people won't be fans of the Oberkommando assassination missions but I like them if for no other reason than you get to revisit and really explore the game's levels without having to spend too much time dicking around during the main story 

+the weapon wheel was really janky to use in the last game for some reason, this one feels way better

+we've all heard the complaints that the story is just a big liberal circle-jerk and for the most part that's bullshit. there's definitely a couple of places where the dialogue gets a little preachy but the vast majority of the story is well thought out, reasonable in its tone, and not cringe-worthy in the slightest 

CONS:

-the main story is a bit too short, and the final boss battle was pretty hard yet strangely not very climactic 

-the difficulty curve is really weird, the game is almost too hard to play during the period where you wear the power armor, and then gets about 200% easier when that ends. it makes sense in the context of the story but it's still frustrating at times

on the whole I'd recommend this game, perhaps it'd be best to get it at a reduced price considering its relatively short length but the overall experience is probably one of the most fun I've had with a FPS in a while. it's got its flaws, and maybe it's not one of the best games of all time, but at the very least it's probably one of the best games of the year.
